title: Practical Artificial Intelligence & AI Productivity
subtitle: Use AI tools confidently, check what they give you, and build routines that save real time.
summary: A hands-on, jargon-free course on using AI chat and image tools for study, work and small business, safely and honestly.
description: Learn what AI really is, how chat assistants work, and how to write prompts that get useful results. You will practise research, writing, planning, small-business and image tasks, learn to protect private information and spot mistakes, and finish by designing an AI workflow for your own work. No technical background is needed, and every exercise can be done with a free tool or on paper.
outcomes: Explain in plain language what AI is, what it is not, and how language models produce answers
Choose the right kind of AI tool for a task and recognise when not to use AI at all
Write clear prompts using context, task, audience, format, constraints and examples, and improve them by iterating
Use AI to research, draft, edit, summarise and study while checking claims against real sources
Apply AI to email, meeting notes, planning and small-business tasks while keeping decisions and promises human
Describe images for AI tools and explain the honesty, copyright, likeness and photo-restoration risks
Protect personal, client and confidential information and write a personal AI-use policy
Design a reusable AI workflow with templates, a review checklist and a measure of time saved
audience: Students and school-leavers who want to use AI honestly and effectively
Office workers and freelancers who want to save time on writing and admin
Small-business owners and side-hustlers handling customers, quotes and social posts
Anyone curious about AI who wants a practical, plain-language starting point
prerequisites: Basic comfort with a web browser and typing; a free AI chat tool is helpful but not required.

modules.title: Understanding artificial intelligence
modules.summary: What AI actually is, what it is not, and why it has suddenly become relevant to ordinary work.
objectives: Explain AI in plain language without hype or jargon
Separate the narrow tools in use today from science-fiction ideas
Recognise AI in everyday tools you already use
Describe why AI matters for ordinary work right now

lessons.title: What AI is, and what it is not

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence is a loose label for software that does tasks we normally think need human judgement: recognising speech, sorting photos, spotting fraud, writing a paragraph. The software is not following a long list of rules that a programmer typed out. It was built by showing a system a very large number of examples until it picked up useful patterns.

That last sentence is the whole trick, and it explains most of what you will learn in this course. Today's AI is pattern-matching at huge scale, packaged so that ordinary people can use it by typing or talking.

blocks.title: Your phone keyboard already does this
blocks.text: When you type a WhatsApp message and your phone offers the next word, it has not understood your message. It has learned which words tend to follow other words. A modern chat assistant is the same basic idea, scaled up enormously and trained on far more text.
What AI is not

items: **Not a mind.** It has no wants, no feelings and no understanding of the way you understand a sentence.
**Not a database of checked facts.** It produces answers that look right based on patterns. Some are wrong.
**Not a person who knows you.** Unless you tell it, it does not know your business, your client or your deadline.
**Not magic.** It is software with clear strengths and clear weaknesses, and you can learn both.

blocks.text: Narrow tools versus the film version

Everything in real use today is narrow AI. It is built for a type of task. A spam filter cannot plan your holiday. A chat assistant can write about almost any topic, yet it cannot tell you reliably whether what it wrote is true.

The movie version, a machine with its own goals or a single system that is an expert at everything, is science fiction. Keeping that distinction in your head protects you from two opposite mistakes: fearing AI as a scheming mind, and trusting it as an all-knowing expert.

blocks.caption: Real tools and imagined ones
rows: Spam filter, voice typing, photo search
Yes, narrow
Dependable at one job, wrong now and then
Chat assistant that drafts and summarises
Yes, flexible but pattern-based
A useful drafting partner whose work needs checking
A machine with its own goals and feelings
No, science fiction
Nothing to plan your week around
One system that is an expert at everything
No, treat such claims with suspicion
Keep the final decision with a person

blocks.title: A working definition
blocks.text: AI is software that has learned patterns from examples and uses them to make a prediction, attach a label or produce new content. It is useful, it is fallible, and it is not a mind.

blocks.prompt: Which statement best describes the AI tools ordinary people use today?
options: Narrow, pattern-based software that is useful but can be wrong
Thinking machines that understand questions the way people do
Databases that only store facts that have been verified
Programs that follow a complete list of rules written by hand
blocks.explain: Today's tools learn patterns from examples. They are useful for specific jobs but they do not understand like a person and they do not guarantee accuracy.

lessons.title: AI you already use, and why it matters now

blocks.text: You have been using AI for years without calling it that. The point of recognising it is practical: once you see how much of it is already in your day, the newer chat tools stop feeling like a strange invention and start looking like the next step.
Everyday examples

items: Your email app moving junk into the spam folder.
A maps app estimating how long the drive will take, including traffic.
Voice typing on your phone and automatic captions on a video.
Your bank flagging a card payment that looks unusual for you.
Photo apps grouping pictures of the same person, or searching for pictures of a beach.
Streaming and shopping apps suggesting what to watch or buy next.

blocks.text: Each of these does one narrow job. None of them chats with you. What changed recently is that tools appeared which handle language so flexibly that you can ask for almost any text task in your own words.
Why it suddenly matters for ordinary work

Much of office and small-business work is language: emails, quotes, summaries, social posts, instructions, notes. A tool that can produce a decent first draft of any of those in seconds changes how long the boring parts take. It does not remove the need for a person to decide what is correct and appropriate. It changes where your time goes.

blocks.title: A plumber in Pretoria
blocks.text: Thandi runs a small plumbing business. Each evening she types quotes into a template and answers WhatsApp questions about availability. With an assistant she pastes in her rough job notes, asks for a clear quote in friendly language, checks the numbers herself, and sends it. Twenty minutes becomes five. The prices, the promises and the final send are still hers.

Three reasons the timing matters. The tools are free or cheap to try. You need no technical skills to start, only the ability to write clearly. And people who learn to use them well will finish certain tasks much faster than people who do not, which is already shaping what employers and clients expect.

blocks.title: Speed is not the same as quality
blocks.text: A fast draft is only worth having if you check it. The rest of this course is about getting the speed without paying for it later in mistakes.

blocks.title: Spot the AI in your day
blocks.intro: You do not need an AI tool for this one. You are training your eye.
tasks: List five places in a normal day where software predicts, sorts, recommends or generates something for you. Use the examples above as a starting point.
For each, write one line on what it learned from (for example, past spam reports or your own viewing history).
Pick one task from your own work or study that is mostly language, such as emails, reports or notes. Write down roughly how long it takes you each week.
If you have a free chat assistant, ask it: 'Explain in three sentences what you can and cannot do.' Read the answer critically.
blocks.reflection: Which of your five examples would you be uncomfortable seeing get things wrong, and why? That discomfort tells you where checking matters most.

blocks.prompt: Why does AI matter now for ordinary workplace tasks?
options: Tools that handle everyday language are cheap to try and need no technical skill
Computers have recently begun to understand and feel as people do
It replaces the need for anyone to check written work before sending
It is only useful to programmers and large companies
blocks.explain: The shift is practical: flexible language tools are easy to access, so routine writing and summarising work can be sped up. People still need to check and decide.

modules.title: How AI systems work (the practical version)
modules.summary: Learning from examples, patterns rather than understanding, and why language models sound confident even when they are wrong.
objectives: Describe how a system learns from examples and what that means for its limits
Distinguish training from using a trained system
Explain in plain words what a language model does when it answers you
Recognise why fluent answers can still be false, and what to do about it

lessons.title: Learning from examples, not from rules

blocks.text: Traditional software follows instructions a programmer wrote. If the email contains this word, do that. For some problems the rules are impossible to write down. Try describing, in exact steps, how to recognise a cat in any photo, or what makes a message sound like a scam. Nobody can list every case.
Machine learning takes a different route. Instead of writing rules, you show the system a large number of examples and let it work out the rules for itself.

blocks.title: How a spam filter gets built
blocks.text: Take thousands of real emails, each labelled by people as spam or not spam. The system tries to sort them, checks its guesses against the labels, and adjusts itself again and again. After enough rounds it has picked up patterns, such as odd wording, suspicious links and urgent money requests. Then it is tested on emails it has never seen.

items.title: Collect examples
items.text: Gather a large set of inputs, usually with the right answers attached.

items.title: Adjust
items.text: The system makes guesses, measures how wrong they are, and tweaks its internal settings to be less wrong.

items.title: Test
items.text: Check it on fresh examples it did not train on, to see if it learned something general.

items.title: Use
items.text: Release it to handle new inputs it has never seen.

blocks.text: Training versus using

The learning happens once, in advance, and it is expensive. That stage is called training. What you do when you type into a chat assistant is using the trained system. In general, your conversation does not retrain it on the spot. Its built-in knowledge stays what it was when training finished.

blocks.caption: Two stages
rows: Who does it
The company that builds the system
You, the person with a question
When
Before release, over a long period
Every time you ask, in seconds
What changes
The system's internal settings
Nothing in the system itself; only the conversation grows
Why it matters to you
Explains its knowledge and its gaps
Explains why you must supply facts it lacks

blocks.text: Patterns, not understanding

A system only learns what its examples show. Imagine training a tool to tell photos of two kinds of animal apart, where one kind was mostly photographed on snow. The tool may quietly learn that snow means that animal. It scores well in testing and fails the first time the animal appears on grass. It found a pattern, just not the one you meant.

blocks.title: The lesson to carry forward
blocks.text: AI is as good as its examples and only inside the situations those examples cover. Outside them it can fail in ways that look strange to a human, and it will not warn you.

blocks.prompt: What is the main difference between traditional software and a machine learning system?
options: Machine learning works out its own patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules
Machine learning needs no data at all before it can work
Traditional software can only be used by programmers
Machine learning always understands the reason behind each answer
blocks.explain: Machine learning systems extract patterns from many examples. Traditional software follows instructions someone wrote, and learning systems do not understand why a pattern holds.

lessons.title: What a language model actually does

blocks.text: Chat assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot are built on language models. A language model has one core skill: given some text, it predicts what text is likely to come next. Then it does that again, and again, one small piece at a time, until it has built a whole reply.

That sounds too simple to explain a tool that can draft a contract clause or explain a maths problem. The reason it works is scale. The model was trained on an enormous amount of writing, so its sense of what usually follows what is very rich.

blocks.label: A tiny illustration of prediction
blocks.text:
Text so far:  Thank you for your
Likely next words:  email / order / patience / feedback / help
Unlikely next words:  giraffe / bicycle

The model picks one, adds it to the text, and predicts again.

blocks.title: Tokens
blocks.text: Models do not read whole words the way you do. They work in tokens, which are chunks of text. A short common word is often a single token, while a long or unusual word may be split into several. You do not need to count tokens. You only need to know that limits on length and cost are measured in them.
What this explains

items: **Why it is so good at tone and structure.** It has seen millions of emails, reports and recipes, so it knows how they usually look.
**Why the same question can give different answers.** There is some controlled randomness in which likely word gets chosen.
**Why it forgets things in a long chat.** It can only consider a limited amount of text at once, called the context window. Details from far back may drop out of view.
**Why it does not know yesterday's news.** Training stops at a cut-off date. Some tools add a web search, but then the quality depends on what it finds.

blocks.text: It also explains why it is better at some jobs than others. Rewriting a rough paragraph in a friendly tone leans on pattern knowledge it has in abundance. Telling you the exact opening hours of your local clinic depends on a fact it may never have seen.

blocks.title: Same prompt, two replies
blocks.text: Ask for a one-line slogan for a bakery in Durban twice. You will almost certainly get two different slogans. Neither is the correct answer, because there is no single correct answer. For creative work that variety is a benefit. For a factual question it is a warning sign.

blocks.title: Watch it predict
blocks.intro: A short experiment you can do with any free chat assistant, or on paper if you have none.
tasks: Type the start of a sentence, such as 'The best thing about load-shedding is', and ask the assistant to continue it in one sentence. Ask again in a new chat.
Compare the two answers. Note what is the same (structure, tone) and what differs (details).
Ask it: 'What was the most recent event you know about?' Note how it describes its own knowledge limits.
No AI tool? Write the start of a sentence on a card, hand it to a friend, and ask them to finish it quickly without thinking too hard. Compare how many different endings you get from three people.
blocks.reflection: If the model builds answers one piece at a time from patterns, what kinds of questions would you expect it to handle well, and which would you double-check?

blocks.prompt: In plain terms, what is a language model doing when it writes a reply?
options: Predicting likely next pieces of text, one after another, from learned patterns
Searching a verified library of facts and quoting the matching entry
Looking up your question in a list of answers written by staff
Reasoning about the world exactly as a human expert would
blocks.explain: A language model generates text by repeatedly predicting what is likely to come next. It is not retrieving a checked answer from a library unless it has been connected to a search tool.

lessons.title: Why it sounds sure and still gets things wrong

blocks.text: A language model is built to produce text that reads well. Reading well and being true are two different things. The model has no built-in fact checker that stops it when it reaches the edge of what it knows. It keeps producing the most plausible-sounding continuation, in the same confident voice.
When that confident text is false, people call it a hallucination. The word is slightly dramatic, but the problem is real.

blocks.title: A made-up source
blocks.text: A student asks an assistant for three academic articles on township tourism, with authors and journal names. The reply lists three neat references. Two of them do not exist. The titles are believable, the authors are plausible, and nothing in the tone hints at a problem. The model produced what a reference list usually looks like.
Where it goes wrong most often

items: Exact figures, dates, quotes, and page numbers.
Sources, references, case law and links it has not actually seen.
Local or niche facts, such as a small town's by-laws or a particular shop's trading hours.
Recent events after its training cut-off.
Anything where you gave it too little to go on and it filled the gap.

blocks.caption: Rough risk guide
rows: Rewrite my paragraph in a friendlier tone
Low
Read it to check it still says what you meant
Summarise text I paste in
Low to medium
Spot-check against the original
Explain a general concept
Medium
Confirm key points with a trusted source
Give me statistics, quotes or references
High
Never use without finding the real source

blocks.text: What you can do about it

First, give it the material. If you paste in the facts, it works from them instead of guessing. Second, ask for plain reasoning and for what it is unsure about, but do not treat its self-assessment as proof. A model can be wrong about its own certainty. Third, verify anything that matters against a source that a person or organisation stands behind.

blocks.title: A useful instinct
blocks.text: The smoother and more specific an unsupported claim sounds, the more reason you have to check it. Precision costs the model nothing.

blocks.title: Catch it out, safely
blocks.intro: Practise checking on something low-stakes where you already know the truth.
tasks: Ask a chat assistant a question about a local topic you know well, such as the history of your suburb, a school, or a nearby business.
Mark each claim as correct, wrong, or unverifiable. Note whether the tone changed between correct and wrong claims.
Now paste in a short paragraph of true facts and ask it to answer from only that text. Compare the accuracy.
No AI tool? Take any answer you have previously received from an assistant and fact-check three claims in it using official websites or a library book.
blocks.reflection: Did the confident tone ever drop when it was wrong? What does that tell you about using tone as a guide to truth?

blocks.prompt: Why do language models sometimes state false things in a confident way?
options: They produce plausible-sounding text and have no automatic check that stops them at the edge of their knowledge
They deliberately mislead users to keep them chatting
They only repeat sentences taken whole from official websites
They are always sure because they have verified every statement
blocks.explain: A model generates likely-sounding text. Fluency is not evidence of truth, so a confident tone says nothing about accuracy.

modules.title: Generative AI: text, images, audio and code
modules.summary: What generative tools can produce, where each kind is strong or weak, and how to decide when to use AI and when not to.
objectives: Describe what generative AI is and name its main output types
Match common tasks to the kind of tool that suits them
Compare general chat assistants with specialised tools
Decide when a task should not be handed to AI

lessons.title: Four kinds of output and what each is good at

blocks.text: Most of the AI you meet in everyday life labels or predicts. Generative AI creates something new in response to your request: a paragraph, a picture, a voice recording, a piece of code. It has learned patterns from huge collections of existing examples and produces fresh output that follows those patterns.
Fresh does not mean original in the human sense, and it does not mean correct. It means newly assembled. Keep both points in mind as we look at each type.

blocks.caption: Four kinds of generative AI
rows: Text
Drafting, rewriting, summarising, brainstorming, changing tone
Exact facts, recent events, precise numbers
Confident errors and invented sources
Images
Concept pictures, mood boards, backgrounds, rough ideas
Readable text inside the image, specific real places, small details such as hands or counts
Faces and logos that resemble real people or brands
Audio
Turning speech into text, voice-overs, background music
Noisy recordings, strong accents, unusual names, people talking over each other
Cloned voices used to deceive
Code
Small scripts, spreadsheet formulas, explaining what code does
Large, carefully secured systems
Code that looks right but fails on real data

blocks.title: A tutor and a spreadsheet
blocks.text: Sipho tutors maths after school and tracks which learners have paid. He asks an assistant for a spreadsheet formula that flags anyone who owes more than R500. The formula it gives looks sensible. He tests it on five invented rows, one of which he knows should be flagged, before trusting it with real learners. The formula had one wrong bracket. Testing caught it in two minutes.
Why the weak spots look the way they do

Because the system works from patterns, it is strongest where patterns are rich and forgiving. Many different emails are acceptable, so drafting one is easy. There is only one right answer to what R4 850 less 12 percent equals, so loose pattern-matching is risky. Pictures work the same way. The tool knows what a bakery counter usually looks like, but it does not count the loaves.

blocks.title: Make it easier to check
blocks.text: Ask for output you can test quickly. A formula you can try on sample rows, a draft you can read in a minute, a summary you can compare to the original. The cheaper a result is to verify, the safer it is to use AI for it.
None of these four types is better than the others. They are different tools with different failure modes. Learning a tool's usual failure mode is the fastest way to use it well.

blocks.prompt: Which task is generative AI generally best suited to?
options: Producing several differently worded drafts of a friendly reminder message
Giving exact legal citations that you will rely on without checking
Counting the objects in a crowded photo with perfect accuracy
Confirming this week's fuel price with certainty
blocks.explain: Drafting varied text is a pattern-rich task where many outputs are acceptable. Exact citations, precise counts and current prices are areas where errors are common and need checking.

lessons.title: Chat assistants, specialised tools, and when not to use AI

blocks.text: There are two broad families of AI tools. A general chat assistant, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot, will try almost anything you type. A specialised tool is built around one job: transcribing meetings, translating, checking grammar, removing a background from a photo, or drafting social posts.

blocks.caption: General and specialised tools
rows: Range
Very wide: text, ideas, explanations, sometimes images and files
Narrow: one task done well
Effort to use
You must explain what you want
Often one click or a template
Typical strength
Flexibility and conversation
Consistency and fit for one workflow
Typical risk
Plausible but wrong answers
Hidden settings and unclear data handling

blocks.text: A sensible rule is to reach for a specialised tool when a job is routine and you do it often, and for a chat assistant when the job is varied or you need to think out loud. Whichever you use, the habits in this course apply equally.
When not to use AI
Knowing when to leave AI out is as valuable as knowing how to use it.

items.title: Is it safe to share?
items.text: If the task needs confidential, personal or client information you may not share, stop or remove those details first.

items.title: Can I check the result?
items.text: If you cannot judge whether the output is right, you cannot safely use it.

items.title: What does a mistake cost?
items.text: A typo in a casual message is cheap. A wrong figure in a quote, a medical instruction or a legal letter is not.

items.title: Is the point to do it myself?
items.text: If you are learning a skill, being assessed, or writing something that must sound personally like you, handing it over defeats the purpose.

blocks.title: Poor fits
blocks.text: Personal messages where your own words matter, such as condolences or an apology. Decisions about people, such as hiring or discipline, made on AI output alone. Medical, legal or financial advice that nobody qualified reviews. Arithmetic you could do on a calculator. Work your school or employer has said must be your own.

blocks.title: Green, amber or red?
blocks.intro: This works on paper, and also with an assistant if you want a second opinion.
tasks: Sort these into green (fine to use AI), amber (use AI but check carefully) or red (do not use, or only with removal of private details): a draft thank-you note to a client; a summary of a public news article; a reply that includes a customer's ID number; an answer to your own assessed assignment; a spreadsheet formula; a performance review for a staff member; the exact VAT on an invoice.
Write one sentence of reasoning next to each choice.
Add two tasks from your own week and sort them as well.
If you used an assistant, compare its suggestions with yours. Where did you disagree, and who had the better argument?
blocks.reflection: What question from the four above did you find yourself asking most often?

blocks.prompt: Which situation is the clearest reason NOT to hand a task to a chat assistant?
options: You are writing a personal apology where your own words matter
You want three alternative subject lines for a newsletter
You need a plain-language summary of a public article
You want help structuring a weekly to-do list
blocks.explain: A personal apology should reflect your voice and sincerity. The other tasks are low-risk drafting or organising jobs where AI help is reasonable.

modules.title: Writing effective prompts
modules.summary: A prompt is a brief. Learn the ingredients of a good one, how to rewrite weak prompts, and how to improve results by iterating.
objectives: Build a prompt from context, task, audience, format, constraints and examples
Rewrite a vague prompt into a specific one
Improve a result through targeted follow-up instead of starting over
Use the assistant to ask you clarifying questions before it drafts

lessons.title: A prompt is a brief: the six ingredients

blocks.text: A prompt is what you type to the AI. The best way to think about it is as a brief you would give to a capable new assistant on their first day. They are clever, they work fast, and they know nothing about your situation. If you say 'write something about our sale', you will get something generic. If you explain who it is for, what you want and what to avoid, you will get something close to usable.

blocks.caption: The six ingredients
rows: Context
What is the situation?
I run a small bakery in Gqeberha and we are launching a Saturday-only sourdough
Task
What exactly should you do?
Write a WhatsApp broadcast announcing it
Audience
Who will read it?
Existing customers, mostly parents, who prefer short messages
Format
What shape should the output take?
Three short lines and one call to action
Constraints
What must or must not appear?
Under 50 words, friendly, no exclamation marks, include the R65 price
Examples
What does good look like?
Here is a previous message that worked well: ...

blocks.text: You will not need all six every time. A quick request for a synonym needs none of them. A message that goes to your customers needs most of them. The skill lies in noticing what is missing that the assistant cannot guess.

blocks.label: A reusable skeleton
blocks.text:
Context: [who you are and the situation]
Task: [what you want done]
Audience: [who will read or use it]
Format: [length, structure, layout]
Constraints: [must include / must avoid / tone]
Example: [optional sample of good output]

blocks.title: Specific beats long
blocks.text: A good prompt is not about length. One precise sentence with the right audience and constraint can beat a vague paragraph. Add detail only where the assistant would otherwise have to guess.
Keep your facts honest

The assistant will happily fill any gaps with invented details, such as a promotion you never offered or an opening time you never gave. State the facts you need to be in the output. Then check that nothing extra slipped in.

blocks.title: Say what you do not want
blocks.text: Telling it to avoid certain words, clichés or claims is often more useful than describing the tone you want. 'No exclamation marks, no jargon' is easier to follow than 'sound professional'.

blocks.prompt: Which addition would most improve the prompt 'Write a post about our new service'?
options: Saying who the service is for, what it does, and how long the post should be
Adding the word 'please' and asking it to try its best
Repeating the request three times in capital letters
Asking it to be more creative without further detail
blocks.explain: Audience, task details and format give the assistant what it would otherwise have to guess. Politeness, repetition and vague requests for creativity do not add information.

lessons.title: Before and after: rewriting weak prompts

blocks.text: The quickest way to learn prompting is to look at weak prompts and fix them. In each pair below, notice what the second version adds that the first leaves the assistant to guess.
Example 1: a customer reply

blocks.label: Before
blocks.text: Reply to this customer complaint.

blocks.label: After
blocks.text: I run a small electrical business in Midrand. A customer says our electrician arrived two hours late and did not call. Write a reply on WhatsApp. Apologise once, explain that traffic and an earlier job overran (do not invent other reasons), offer a R150 discount on the next visit, and ask if they would like to rebook. Keep it under 80 words, warm but not grovelling.

The first prompt forces the assistant to invent the story, the tone and the offer. The second carries your facts, your decision about the discount, and a limit on length. You are still deciding what happens. The assistant is only helping with the wording.
Example 2: a study summary

blocks.label: Before
blocks.text: Summarise this chapter.

blocks.label: After
blocks.text: I am a first-year student revising for a test on Friday. Summarise the text below into five key ideas, each with a one-sentence plain-language explanation and one everyday example. Then give me three short questions I can use to test myself. Text: [paste chapter]
Example 3: a plan

blocks.label: Before
blocks.text: Help me plan my week.

blocks.label: After
blocks.text: I freelance as a photographer and also have a day job on weekdays until 17:00. This week I must edit 40 wedding photos by Thursday, invoice two clients, and shoot a family session on Saturday morning. Load-shedding may cut evening editing time. Suggest a day-by-day plan with realistic time blocks, and flag anything that looks too tight.

blocks.title: What changed in every case
blocks.text: The strong prompts say who you are, what the real situation is, what output you want, and what limits apply. None of them is clever. They are simply complete.

blocks.title: Rewrite three prompts
blocks.intro: You can do this on paper first and test it with an assistant afterwards.
tasks: Choose three prompts you have used, or would use: for instance 'write an email to my landlord', 'explain budgeting' and 'give me content ideas'.
Rewrite each using at least four of the six ingredients. Include one real fact and one constraint in each.
If you have a free assistant, run both versions of one prompt and compare the results side by side.
Save your best rewrite as a template by replacing the specific details with square brackets.
blocks.reflection: What details did you have to go and find out before you could write the better prompt? Those gaps are what the assistant would otherwise have guessed.

blocks.prompt: What is the main reason the 'After' customer-reply prompt works better than the 'Before' version?
options: It supplies the facts, the decision and the limits, so the assistant does not have to invent them
It uses longer sentences, which the assistant prefers
It avoids mentioning the customer's complaint
It leaves the offer and the tone for the assistant to choose
blocks.explain: A better prompt carries the real situation, your decisions and the constraints. The assistant should polish wording, not invent facts or make promises on your behalf.

lessons.title: Iterate, and let the AI interview you

blocks.text: Almost nobody gets the best result from the first prompt. Treat the first reply as a rough draft and shape it with follow-up instructions. This is faster than starting from scratch, and the conversation keeps the context you have already given.
Give feedback the way an editor would

blocks.caption: Vague and useful feedback
rows: Make it better
Cut it to 60 words and put the price in the first line
Sounds wrong
Too formal. We say 'hi' not 'dear customer'. Rewrite as if texting a regular
Not what I wanted
I wanted three options, each with a different opening. Keep the facts the same
More professional
Remove the slang and the exclamation marks, keep the warmth

blocks.text: Change one or two things at a time so that you can tell what helped. If a chat has become tangled, start a fresh one and paste in the best version so far.
Ask it to ask you questions

When a task is big or you are unsure what to include, flip the roles. Tell the assistant to interview you first. It will ask for the facts it needs, and you will notice which of them you had not thought about.

blocks.label: Interview prompt
blocks.text: I need to write a quote for a client who wants her lounge repainted. Before you write anything, ask me up to six questions about what you need to know. Ask them one at a time and wait for my answers. Then draft the quote and list any assumptions you made.

blocks.title: Why this works
blocks.text: A freelance photographer asks for help with a proposal. The assistant asks about the shoot date, hours, number of edited images, travel costs and deposit terms. Two of those were missing from her own notes. The interview exposed the gaps before a client did.

blocks.title: Keep a prompt log
blocks.text: When a prompt works, copy it into a note with a title. Within a month you will have a small personal library, and most of your future prompts will be edits of past ones.

blocks.prompt: A reply is nearly right but too formal. What is the most effective next step?
options: Tell the assistant exactly what to change, such as the tone and an example of how you speak
Close the chat and write the whole message again without help
Type 'try again' repeatedly until a better one appears
Ask for the same text but with the word 'better' added
blocks.explain: Specific feedback keeps the useful parts and corrects the problem. Vague retries leave the assistant guessing again.

modules.title: AI for research and writing
modules.summary: A safe research workflow, checking claims against real sources, and drafting and studying with AI while keeping your own voice and honesty.
objectives: Follow a research workflow that uses AI as a guide, not as a source
Check claims against real sources and cite the sources you actually used
Use AI to edit and improve drafts while keeping your own voice
Use AI to study and summarise without losing accuracy

lessons.title: A safe research workflow

blocks.text: Research is where AI is both most tempting and most dangerous. It can explain unfamiliar topics in seconds, and it can also hand you invented facts that read perfectly well. The fix is to change what you ask it to be. Use it as a guide to the topic, never as the source of the facts you rely on.

items.title: Write your question
items.text: State what you need to find out and why. A sharp question gets you a better search than a vague topic.

items.title: Get oriented
items.text: Ask the assistant to explain the topic simply, list key terms, and suggest what you should look up. Treat this as a map, not as findings.

items.title: Find real sources
items.text: Search for official websites, textbooks, journals, news organisations and the people who actually know. Open them yourself.

items.title: Work from the text
items.text: Paste short passages from those sources into the assistant and ask for summaries or comparisons. Now it is working from material you chose.

items.title: Verify
items.text: Check any figure, date, quote or rule against the original source before it goes into your work.

items.title: Write it up
items.text: Put things in your own words, and cite the sources you used.

blocks.title: A tax threshold
blocks.text: Lindiwe is a freelancer asking about the income level at which she must register for a tax. An assistant gives a clear-sounding figure. Tax thresholds change and differ by country, and the assistant may be using old information. She uses the answer only to learn the terms, then finds the current figure on the revenue authority's own website and quotes that.
What counts as a source

blocks.caption: Trust ladder
rows: Official body, law, original data
Highest
Cite the document itself, with the date
Textbook, peer-reviewed journal, established news outlet
High
Check the publication date and who wrote it
Company marketing, personal blog, social media post
Use with care
Ask who gains if you believe it
AI chat output
Not a source
Use it to find sources and ideas, then confirm elsewhere

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: If a claim matters enough to appear in your work, it matters enough to trace to something a person or organisation stands behind.
Some assistants can browse the web and show links. That helps, but it does not remove the need to check. Open the link, find the passage, and confirm it says what the assistant claims it says.

blocks.prompt: In a safe research workflow, what role should an AI assistant play?
options: A guide for getting oriented and summarising passages you chose, not the source of the facts you rely on
The final authority whose statements you cite directly
A replacement for looking at any official or published material
A way to skip checking figures and dates
blocks.explain: AI is good at explaining and organising. The facts you rely on should come from sources you have opened and verified.

lessons.title: Checking claims and citing honestly

blocks.text: Checking is a skill, and it is quicker than most people expect. You do not have to re-research everything. You have to find the claims that could hurt you if they were wrong, and test those.
A fast claim check

items: Underline every checkable claim: numbers, dates, names, quotes, rules, and 'studies show' statements.
Sort them: which would embarrass you or cause harm if wrong? Check those first.
Search for each one separately in a source you trust. Do not just ask the same assistant 'are you sure?'
If you cannot confirm it, cut it, soften it, or say plainly that you could not verify it.

blocks.title: Asking the same tool to confirm itself
blocks.text: An assistant that invented a statistic will often agree that it is correct when you ask. Treat its reassurance as a prompt to go and look elsewhere, never as the check itself.
Citing: honesty about what you used

Cite the sources you actually opened and read. Do not cite a reference because an assistant produced it. If a reference came from AI and you cannot find it, it may not exist. A made-up reference in a report or assignment looks like deliberate fabrication, whatever your intent.

Be open about AI use where it is expected. Many schools, universities and employers have rules about how and when AI may be used and how it must be acknowledged. Find the rule for your situation. If you are unsure, ask. Passing off AI-written text as your own unaided work, or presenting unchecked AI claims as fact, is the quick way to lose someone's trust.

blocks.caption: What to do in common situations
rows: School or university assignment
Follow the course policy; note AI help if asked; never submit AI text as your own work if that is prohibited
Report for your manager
Check the facts, and say if AI helped when it matters to how the report is relied on
Blog or social media post
You are responsible for every claim, whatever tool drafted it
A quote you want to use
Find it in the original source, not in an AI answer

blocks.title: Audit an AI paragraph
blocks.intro: Practise checking without needing to trust anything.
tasks: Ask a chat assistant for a 150-word paragraph on a topic you are interested in, including at least five specific facts or figures. If you have no AI tool, take a paragraph from any online summary or a social media post instead.
Underline every checkable claim. Number them.
Find a trustworthy source for each claim and write beside it: confirmed, wrong, or could not find.
Rewrite the paragraph keeping only what you confirmed. Add the sources you used.
blocks.reflection: How many claims survived? Which kind of claim was hardest to verify, and what does that tell you about where to be most careful?

blocks.prompt: An assistant gives you a reference you cannot find online. What should you do?
options: Leave it out, because you cannot confirm it exists
Include it, since the assistant sounded certain
Include it but change the author's name so it looks more plausible
Ask the assistant to confirm and cite it if it says yes
blocks.explain: An unverifiable reference may be invented. Only cite what you have opened and read, and never rely on the assistant to confirm its own output.

lessons.title: Drafting, editing and studying with your own voice

blocks.text: The best use of AI in writing is as a sharp editor and a patient practice partner. The weakest is as a ghostwriter that you let speak for you. Writing that is entirely generated tends to be bland and slightly off. Readers notice, and it also does not sound like you.
Draft first, then ask for help
Start with your own rough version, even if it is messy. You supply the ideas, the facts and the point of view. Then use the assistant for jobs that improve the writing without replacing it.

items: Ask it to list the five weakest sentences and say why, then fix them yourself.
Ask it to cut your text by a third without changing the meaning.
Ask it to check for confusing order, repeated points or missing steps.
Ask for two or three alternative openings, then choose and adapt one.

blocks.label: Voice-keeping prompt
blocks.text:
Here are two short pieces I wrote, so you can see how I write: [paste samples].
Below is a rough draft. Edit it for clarity and flow only. Keep my wording where it already works, keep my facts exactly as they are, and mark any place where you changed the meaning. Do not add new claims.

Draft: [paste draft]

blocks.title: Spot the sameness
blocks.text: If you ask for several pieces in a row, watch for the same favourite phrases showing up in each. Cut them. Your own specific details are what make writing sound like a person.
Studying and summarising

AI can also help you learn. Paste in your own notes or a passage you are allowed to use, and ask for a summary, a simpler explanation, or practice questions. A summary can leave out something that matters, so compare it with the original before you rely on it for a test.

blocks.label: Study prompt
blocks.text: Here are my notes on [topic]. 1) Summarise them in five bullet points. 2) Explain the hardest idea as if I am new to it, with an everyday example. 3) Ask me five questions one at a time, wait for my answer, and tell me what I missed.

blocks.title: Explain it back
blocks.text: A learner finishes a chapter and writes a short explanation from memory. Then she asks the assistant to point out what is missing or wrong in her version. This works better than reading a summary, because she has to produce the idea herself.

blocks.prompt: Which approach to writing with AI is most likely to keep your own voice?
options: Write a rough draft yourself, then ask the assistant to edit for clarity while keeping your wording and facts
Ask it to write the whole piece, then submit it unchanged
Ask for ten different versions and mix random sentences from each
Paste in a topic and let it decide the argument
blocks.explain: Starting from your own draft keeps your ideas and voice. The assistant then improves clarity rather than replacing you.

modules.title: AI for productivity and planning
modules.summary: Practical routines for email, meeting notes, messy notes, weekly planning and learning a new topic faster.
objectives: Triage an inbox and draft replies from your own bullet points
Turn meeting notes or messy text into decisions, actions and owners
Build a realistic weekly plan with AI while keeping the final decisions
Use AI to learn a new topic faster without trusting it blindly

lessons.title: Email triage and replies

blocks.text: Email is a natural fit for AI because it is mostly language, much of it routine. The aim is not to stop reading your mail. The aim is to spend your attention on the messages that need judgement, and to spend less time wording the ones that do not.
Triage

Paste in a batch of subject lines and the first sentence of each, with anything private removed. Ask the assistant to sort them. You are not asking it to decide what matters to you. You are asking it for a first pass that you can overrule.

blocks.label: Triage prompt
blocks.text:
Below are 15 email subject lines with their first sentences. Sort them into: 1) needs a reply today, 2) needs a reply this week, 3) for information only, 4) probably ignorable. Give a one-line reason for each. If you cannot tell, say so rather than guessing.

[paste]
Replies from your own bullets
The reliable pattern is to give the decision and the facts in rough bullet points, and let the assistant turn them into polite, clear sentences. You make the decision. It handles the phrasing.

blocks.label: Reply prompt
blocks.text:
Write a short, friendly reply to the email below. My decisions: yes to a call on Thursday after 14:00, no to the Friday deadline, and I need the signed form first. Keep it under 90 words. Do not promise anything else.

Email: [paste]

blocks.title: After a long load-shedding day
blocks.text: Zanele, a freelance bookkeeper, has twenty-two unread emails and two hours of power left on her laptop. She pastes the subject lines, finds three that need replies today, and writes three sets of bullets. Ten minutes later three short, courteous replies are ready for her to read, adjust and send.

blocks.caption: Who does what
rows: Sorts and summarises
Decide what is urgent in your real situation
Turns bullets into clear sentences
Provide the facts, prices and promises
Adjusts tone: warmer, firmer, shorter
Read every word before sending
Suggests a subject line
Check names, dates, amounts and attachments

blocks.title: Do not paste everything
blocks.text: Emails often contain other people's personal details, account numbers or confidential matters. Remove or replace them first, and check what your workplace allows. Module 9 covers this in detail.

blocks.prompt: What is the most reliable way to use AI to write an email reply?
options: Give it your decision and key facts in bullet points and have it phrase them, then read the result before sending
Paste the email and send whatever it returns without reading
Ask it to decide what you should agree to
Let it add any details it thinks sound good
blocks.explain: You supply the decisions and facts. The assistant helps with wording, and you review the result because you are accountable for what you send.

lessons.title: Meeting notes and messy notes into structure

blocks.text: Most notes are messy because they were written fast. AI is good at imposing order on text you already have, which is a lower-risk job than producing facts from nothing. The material is yours, so you can check the result against it.
Meeting notes

Start with your own jottings or a transcript. If a meeting is recorded or transcribed, tell the other people and follow your organisation's rules. Some people do not want to be recorded, and some meetings are confidential.

items.title: Paste the raw notes
items.text: Include whatever you have, however rough. Remove names or figures that should not leave your organisation.

items.title: Ask for a fixed structure
items.text: Decisions made, actions with owner and due date, open questions, and a three-line summary.

items.title: Tell it not to invent
items.text: Where an owner or date is missing, it must write 'not stated' rather than guess.

items.title: Check against the notes
items.text: Make sure each action matches what was said, then send.

blocks.label: Before: raw notes
blocks.text: mon mtg w/ Pieter + Aisha. stock count fri? Aisha says supplier late again. Pieter wants new supplier quotes, maybe 3. website banner needs changing b4 month end. who does invoices?? decided: no new hires till Jan.

blocks.label: After: structured
blocks.text:
Decisions
- No new hires until January.

Actions
- Get quotes from up to three new suppliers: Pieter, due date not stated
- Update website banner: owner not stated, before month end
- Stock count: Friday (confirm who)

Open questions
- Who handles invoices?
- Does Aisha's supplier delay change the stock count date?

blocks.title: The prompt that prevents the worst error
blocks.text: Always add: 'If an owner, date or number is not in my notes, write not stated. Do not guess.' Otherwise assistants tend to fill gaps with believable guesses, and a wrong owner on an action item causes real trouble.
Other messy-text jobs

items: A page of voice-note transcription into a tidy checklist.
A rambling customer message into three clear questions to answer.
A pile of ideas into a grouped list with duplicates merged.

blocks.title: Tidy a real mess
blocks.intro: Use your own notes, or the sample above if you want a safe example.
tasks: Take a page of rough notes from a recent meeting, class or phone call. Remove names, numbers and anything private.
Write a prompt that asks for decisions, actions with owner and due date, and open questions, and tells the assistant to write 'not stated' for gaps.
Run it, then compare the result with your original line by line. Mark anything the assistant changed or invented.
No AI tool? Do the restructuring by hand using the three headings above, and time yourself.
blocks.reflection: Which part of the structured version would you have missed if you had only skimmed it?

blocks.prompt: Why add 'write not stated if information is missing' when asking for action items?
options: It stops the assistant from guessing owners or dates that were never mentioned
It makes the assistant write longer summaries
It lets the assistant skip checking your notes
It improves the grammar of the output
blocks.explain: Without that instruction a model may fill gaps with plausible guesses. A clear 'not stated' makes missing information visible so a person can resolve it.

lessons.title: Weekly planning and learning a new topic faster

blocks.text: Planning is another job where the assistant organises and you decide. It cannot know your energy, your family commitments or how long a task really takes you. You can tell it, though, and it can then lay the pieces out more sensibly than a blank page does.
A planning conversation

blocks.label: Weekly plan prompt
blocks.text: Here is my week. Fixed commitments: work 08:00 to 17:00 Mon to Fri, school pick-up at 14:30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Must finish: a presentation by Thursday, two invoices by Wednesday, and a first draft of my CV. I focus best in the early morning. Evening power cuts may remove 2 hours some nights. Draft a day-by-day plan with realistic blocks, a buffer each day, and tell me which items look too tight.

Read the plan critically. Assistants are often too optimistic about time. If it has scheduled four hours of focused work in a day that is already full, say so and ask it to rebalance. Then copy the final version into your own calendar or notebook, because that is where you will actually look.

blocks.title: Break big jobs down
blocks.text: Ask: 'Break this task into steps of 30 minutes or less, in order, and tell me what I need before each step.' A vague project like 'sort out my taxes' becomes a short list that you can start in the next ten minutes.
Learning a new topic faster

Used well, an assistant works like a patient tutor available at any hour. Used badly, it hands you a pile of confident half-truths. The difference is that you stay in charge of the learning and check anything important.

items: Ask for a map: the main ideas, in a sensible order, for a complete beginner.
Ask what beginners usually get wrong or confuse.
Ask for one simple analogy per idea, then judge whether it holds up.
Practise: have it quiz you one question at a time and explain your mistakes.
Confirm the key facts with a textbook, a course or an official source.

blocks.title: Learning spreadsheets
blocks.text: Kagiso wants to use spreadsheets for his side-hustle stock list. He asks for a four-week plan at thirty minutes a day. He follows it, asks the assistant to quiz him on formulas, and checks anything unfamiliar in the spreadsheet program's own help pages. After a month he can build the sheet himself.

blocks.prompt: An assistant's weekly plan packs six hours of focused work into a day you described as already full. What should you do?
options: Tell it the plan is unrealistic and ask it to rebalance with buffers
Follow the plan exactly because the assistant is good at maths
Delete your other commitments
Ask it to schedule more tasks so you finish earlier
blocks.explain: You know your real capacity. Assistants tend to be optimistic, so correct the plan with specific feedback, and keep the final say yourself.

modules.title: AI for small businesses
modules.summary: Customer replies, product descriptions, social posts, quotes, simple procedures and FAQs, plus what a small business should always keep human.
objectives: Draft customer replies and FAQ answers that stay accurate to your business
Produce product descriptions and social posts without inventing claims
Structure quotes, proposals and simple procedures with AI help
Decide which business tasks should always stay with a person

lessons.title: Customer replies and FAQs

blocks.text: Small businesses answer the same questions again and again. What time do you open? How much for this? Can you come on Saturday? What happens if I need to cancel? Each answer takes a minute, and those minutes add up to hours. AI is well suited to this, as long as the facts stay yours.
Build a facts-and-voice sheet once
Before asking for any replies, write a short note that you can paste at the start of a chat. It holds the things the assistant cannot know and should never invent.

blocks.label: Facts-and-voice sheet (example: a bakery)
blocks.text:
Business: Lekker Loaf, small home bakery in Bloemfontein.
Hours: Tue to Sat, 07:00 to 14:00. Closed Sunday and Monday.
Orders: custom cakes need 5 days notice and a 50% deposit.
Delivery: within 10 km, R60. Otherwise collection only.
Allergens: we use wheat, eggs, milk and nuts in the same kitchen. Never state that anything is allergen-free.
Voice: warm, brief, first names, no exclamation marks, English with the odd Afrikaans word.
With that sheet in the conversation, you can paste a customer's message and ask for a reply. The assistant works from your facts instead of guessing.

blocks.title: An electrician's reply
blocks.text: Pieter, an electrician, gets a WhatsApp asking whether he can fix a tripping DB board today. His facts sheet says he is booked until Thursday for non-emergencies. The draft politely offers Thursday morning, asks for a photo of the board, and says nothing about the cause. He added one line himself: if there is a burning smell, switch off the main supply and call him. He did not want the assistant making that safety call for him.
Turn real questions into an FAQ

Collect the ten questions customers ask most, from your own messages. Ask the assistant to write a clear answer to each using only your facts sheet, and to put 'ask the owner' where your facts do not cover the question. Read each answer against what you actually do.

blocks.caption: Reply types and how much care they need
rows: Simple enquiry (hours, price, availability)
Draft and send quickly after checking
Make sure prices and dates are yours
Delay or reschedule
Draft an honest, courteous note
Do not let it invent reasons
Complaint or refund
Help with wording only
Decide the outcome yourself and read every word
Anything about safety or health
Very little
Say it yourself or have a qualified person review it

blocks.title: Never let it speak for you on allergens or safety
blocks.text: A cheerful draft might say a product is nut-free or a wiring job is safe. If you did not tell it so, it should not say so. Add rules like this to the facts sheet and check every reply.

blocks.prompt: Why create a facts-and-voice sheet for your business?
options: It gives the assistant your real details and tone so it does not invent policies or prices
It lets the assistant decide your policies for you
It makes replies longer
It is required before any AI tool will work
blocks.explain: The sheet supplies facts the assistant cannot know. This keeps replies accurate and in your voice, but you still review them.

lessons.title: Product descriptions and social posts

blocks.text: Writing about your own products is oddly hard. You know them so well that you forget what a new customer needs to hear. An assistant gives you a starting draft in seconds, and you edit it into something true.
Start with facts, then ask for words

Give it the real details: what the product is, size, materials or ingredients, price, who it is for, and what makes it different. Ask for two or three options in different tones. Then delete anything that is not true.

blocks.label: Product description prompt
blocks.text: Write two short product descriptions (under 60 words each) for a hand-poured soy candle, 200 g, burns about 40 hours, scents: lavender and rooibos, R145, made in Pietermaritzburg. For gift buyers. Use only the facts I gave you. Do not claim health benefits or use the word 'eco-friendly'.

blocks.caption: Four small businesses, four uses
rows: Home bakery
Menu descriptions and a Saturday WhatsApp broadcast
Ingredients, allergens, prices, collection times
Electrician
A short 'what we do' page and a post about winter safety checks
Any safety or compliance wording, which must come from you
Freelance photographer
Package descriptions and captions for a portfolio post
What each package really includes, and permission to post client photos
Tutoring side-hustle
A flyer and a welcome message to parents
Subjects, grades, rates, and no claims about guaranteed results

blocks.title: The claim check
blocks.text: AI loves persuasive phrases: best in town, guaranteed results, 100 percent natural, award-winning. If you cannot prove it, cut it. Untrue claims can damage trust and, in some cases, break advertising rules.
Social posts without sounding robotic

Ask for post ideas, not finished posts. Pick one, then rewrite it in how you actually speak. Add the specific detail only you have: the customer who always orders the same loaf, the photo from this morning's job. That detail is what people respond to.

blocks.title: A batch day
blocks.text: Spend 30 minutes once a week asking for a week of post ideas based on your facts sheet. Choose three, edit them, and schedule them. This is easier than inventing something every morning.

blocks.title: A tutor's post
blocks.text: Naledi tutors maths for Grade 8 and 9. Her first draft promised 'guaranteed distinctions'. She removed it. Her final post said what she does: weekly small-group sessions, past-paper practice, and a short progress note to parents each month.

blocks.prompt: A draft product description says your candle is 'eco-friendly and award-winning'. You have never made either claim. What should you do?
options: Remove the claims, because you cannot support them
Keep them, since they sound appealing
Keep them but make the text smaller
Ask the assistant to say they are proven
blocks.explain: Marketing claims must be true. Remove anything you cannot back up, however good it sounds.

lessons.title: Quotes, simple procedures and what to keep human

blocks.text: Quotes, proposals and written procedures share a pattern: the structure is repetitive and the content is yours. That makes them a good fit for AI. The assistant provides a clean layout and clear wording. You provide the numbers, terms and promises.
Quotes and proposals

blocks.label: Quote structure prompt
blocks.text: I am a freelance photographer. Draft a one-page quote for a 4-hour family shoot. Use these details only: R2 800 for the session, 30 edited images delivered online within 14 days, R400 extra for a printed album, 50% deposit to secure the date, balance due on the day. Include a short friendly introduction, a clear list of what is included and not included, and a line asking the client to reply to confirm. Do not add terms I have not listed.

Check every figure and date on the result. Then ask yourself what is missing: travel, cancellation, what happens if it rains. Add those from your own policy. For larger contracts, have a qualified person review the final wording.
Simple procedures (SOPs)

A standard operating procedure is a written way of doing a routine job, so that someone else could do it the same way. Small businesses often keep these in their heads. An assistant can help you get them onto a page.

blocks.title: A fast way to write one

items.title: Talk it out
items.text: Describe the job aloud or in rough bullets, exactly as you do it, including the awkward bits.

items.title: Ask for numbered steps
items.text: Have the assistant turn it into clear steps and a short 'before you start' list.

items.title: Mark gaps
items.text: Tell it to flag anything unclear rather than fill it in.

items.title: Test it
items.text: Ask someone who has never done the job to follow it. Fix every place they stumble.

blocks.text: What to keep human

items: Prices, discounts, deadlines and any other promise made in your name.
Safety, legal, health and compliance statements.
How to settle a serious complaint or refund.
Anything involving a customer's private details, unless you have removed them.
Relationships: the personal call, the thank-you, the apology.

blocks.title: Your business starter kit
blocks.intro: Use your own business, a side-hustle, or one you would like to start.
tasks: Write a facts-and-voice sheet of about 100 words: what you sell, prices, hours, policies, and three rules about what must never be claimed.
Pick one customer message you often receive. Write a prompt that uses your sheet and asks for a reply, then check the draft against your facts.
Choose one routine job and write it as a procedure draft, using the four steps above.
No AI tool? Write the sheet and the procedure by hand, and write the reply yourself in two versions, one short and one warmer.
blocks.reflection: Which line in your facts sheet prevented the most potential mistakes?

blocks.prompt: Which task should stay with a person in a small business?
options: Deciding how to settle a serious customer complaint
Turning bullet points into a tidy checklist
Suggesting three subject lines for a newsletter
Reformatting a list of products as a table
blocks.explain: Settling a complaint involves judgement, empathy and promises made in your name. Formatting and suggestion tasks are suitable for AI support.

modules.title: AI image generation and creative content
modules.summary: How image tools respond to prompts, how to iterate, and how to stay honest about copyright, likeness and the limits of enhancing real photos.
objectives: Describe an image to an AI tool using subject, style, light and composition
Iterate on an image by changing one thing at a time
Decide when AI images are suitable for ideas and when they are not suitable as final work
Explain the honesty, copyright, likeness and photo-restoration risks of AI-made and AI-edited images

lessons.title: Describing the picture you want

blocks.text: An image generator takes a written description and produces a picture that matches the patterns it learned from a very large number of captioned images. Like a chat assistant, it cannot read your mind. If you type 'a cake', you will get the most average cake imaginable. If you describe the cake, the room and the mood, you get something far closer to what you had in your head.
The good news is that you do not need artistic vocabulary. You need to answer four plain questions.

blocks.caption: Four things to describe
rows: Subject
What is in the picture, and what is it doing?
A baker dusting flour over a tray of rusks
Style
What kind of image is it?
Documentary photograph, flat vector illustration, watercolour, simple icon
Light and colour
What is the lighting and mood?
Soft morning window light, warm tones, a little steam
Composition
Where is the camera and what is the framing?
Close-up from the side, shallow focus, empty space at the top for a headline

blocks.label: Weak and stronger image prompts
blocks.text:
Weak:
A bakery.

Stronger:
A small home bakery kitchen in the early morning. A baker in an apron dusts flour over a tray of rusks on a wooden table. Soft window light, warm colours, documentary photograph style. Shot from the side at table height, shallow focus, space at the top of the frame for text.
Notice that the stronger prompt says nothing technical. It says what you would tell a photographer arriving to shoot the scene.
Iterate one change at a time

The first image is rarely the one you keep. Look at what is wrong and change one thing: the light, the style, or the framing. If you change everything at once, you cannot tell what helped. Most tools let you generate several versions of the same prompt, which is a quick way to see the range.

blocks.title: A flyer for a Saturday market
blocks.text: Zodwa sells handmade soap and needs a background for a flyer. Her first prompt produced a glossy, crowded scene with strange blurry lettering on the bottles. She asked for a plain flat illustration with a pale background and no text, then added the words herself in a free design app. The AI gave her the picture. She supplied the letters, because image tools often struggle to produce readable text.

blocks.title: Say what to leave out
blocks.text: If your tool allows it, state what you do not want: no text, no people, no logos, no clutter. Fewer elements usually means fewer odd details.
Ideas versus final work

AI images are excellent for exploring: mood boards, rough concepts, colour ideas, and options to show a client before committing to a real photo shoot. They are riskier as finished work when the image has to show your actual product, your actual premises or a real person. A picture of a cake the tool invented is not a picture of your cake, and customers who receive something different have a fair complaint.

blocks.prompt: A first image comes out with the wrong lighting but the right subject and framing. What is the best next step?
options: Change only the lighting description and generate again
Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch with new subject and style
Add several unrelated changes in the same attempt
Give up, because the tool cannot adjust light
blocks.explain: Changing one element at a time shows you what influenced the result. Rewriting everything makes it hard to know what worked.

lessons.title: Honesty, copyright and likeness

blocks.text: Making an image takes seconds, which makes it easy to skip the questions that matter. Three of them come up again and again: is it clear the picture is AI-made, who owns it, and whose face or style is in it?
Honesty about what the image is

An AI image is an illustration of something imagined, not a record of something that happened. Problems start when people treat it as a record. A made-up photo of a 'happy customer', a fake testimonial portrait, or a picture of a building project that was never built can mislead the people who see it.

items: Do not present an AI picture as a real photograph of a real event, person or product.
Do not use invented people as if they were your actual clients, staff or reviewers.
Where it matters, label the image. A short note such as 'AI-generated illustration' is enough.
Follow the rules of your school, employer or platform. Many ask for disclosure, and some competitions and publications ban AI images outright.

blocks.text: Copyright

Copyright rules for AI-generated material are still being argued in courts and parliaments, and they differ from country to country. Do not rely on a confident claim from a chat or a website about who owns an image. For commercial work, read the terms of the tool you use, which say what you may do with the output. If you need certainty, ask someone qualified.

A safer habit is to avoid copying. Do not ask for an image 'in the style of' a named living artist so that you can sell something that looks like their work, and do not feed in someone else's artwork or photographs without permission.
Likeness
A real person's face, voice and name belong to them in a way that matters. Making pictures of real people doing things they never did can hurt them, even when you mean it as a joke.

blocks.title: People are not raw material
blocks.text: Do not generate or alter images of a real person without their permission, and never create anything that could embarrass, impersonate or sexualise someone. Do not upload photographs of children or of other people's faces into a tool unless you are allowed to and you know how the tool handles them. Module 9 returns to deepfakes.

blocks.caption: Quick decisions
rows: Illustrating a blog post with a general concept
Fine. Consider a short label that it is AI-made.
A product photo for your shop
Use a real photo of the real product.
A portrait of a satisfied client
Use a real photo with their consent, or no portrait.
A meme using a classmate's face
Do not. Ask yourself how they would feel, and whether they agreed.

blocks.prompt: A small shop wants a picture of a happy customer for its website. What is the honest approach?
options: Use a real photograph taken with the customer's consent, or use no portrait
Generate a face with AI and present it as a real customer
Take a stranger's photo from social media without asking
Use an AI face and quote an invented testimonial beside it
blocks.explain: An AI-made face is not a real customer, and presenting it as one misleads viewers. A real photo with consent keeps the claim true.

lessons.title: Restoring and enhancing real photos without inventing the past

blocks.text: Many people first meet AI image tools when they want to fix an old photograph: sharpen a blurry wedding picture, colour a black-and-white portrait of a grandparent, or clear up a scanned school photo. The results can be striking. They can also be wrong in a way that is hard to see.

When a photo is blurry or damaged, the detail is simply not in the file. The tool fills the gap by predicting what such a face, fabric or building would usually look like. That prediction is plausible. It is not a record of what was actually there.

blocks.title: Grandfather's new face
blocks.text: Sizwe uploads a faded 1970s portrait of his grandfather and asks an enhancer to sharpen it. The new version looks crisp. His aunt looks at it and says it is not him. The tool had given him a slightly different nose, smoother skin, and teeth that were never in the original. It looked better and showed someone who did not exist.
What can be invented

items: Facial features, expressions, teeth, hair, and the exact shape of eyes and mouths.
Writing, signs, badges and numbers, which may become neat but meaningless.
Colours in a black-and-white photo, such as clothing, skin tone and a car's paint.
Objects and background details that were too blurry to see.

items.title: Keep the original
items.text: Always save an untouched copy of the scan or file before you try anything.

items.title: Choose the lightest fix
items.text: Cleaning scratches, adjusting brightness and gentle sharpening change less than full AI enhancement.

items.title: Compare side by side
items.text: Look at features that matter: faces, hands, text, medals, dates. Ask people who knew the subject if you can.

items.title: Label the result
items.text: Note that the image has been enhanced or coloured by AI, especially if it will be shared or archived.

items.title: Never use it as evidence
items.text: Do not use an enhanced image to identify a person, prove an event or settle a dispute.

blocks.title: Enhanced is not the same as recovered
blocks.text: An AI-enhanced photo is an interpretation. It may be lovely and useful for a family album. It is not a more accurate version of the past, and it should not be treated as one.

blocks.title: Compare original and enhanced
blocks.intro: Use a photo you own and have the right to edit. Avoid photographs of other people's faces unless they agree.
tasks: Choose one old or low-quality image of an object, a place or a pet, or a photo of yourself.
Save a copy of the original. If you have an AI enhancer or generator, run the copy through it once.
Zoom in on the original and the result side by side. List every difference you can find: shape, colour, text, texture.
Mark each difference as 'was visible in the original' or 'invented by the tool'.
No AI tool? Do the same exercise with a photocopy and a pen: sketch what you believe is hidden in a smudged area, then list what you are guessing.
blocks.reflection: Which of the invented details would have been easiest to accept without noticing, and what would you tell someone who wanted to use the enhanced image as proof?

blocks.prompt: Why can an AI-enhanced version of a blurry old portrait be misleading?
options: The tool fills missing detail with plausible guesses, which may differ from the real person
It always makes faces older than they were
It recovers the exact original pixels that the camera lost
It cannot change the image at all
blocks.explain: When detail is missing from the file, enhancement tools predict what is probably there. The result can look convincing and still show features that were never in the photograph.

modules.title: Privacy, limitations and responsible AI use
modules.summary: What never to paste into an AI tool, how bias, hallucination and deepfakes can hurt you, and how to write a simple personal AI-use policy.
objectives: Identify the kinds of information that should not be pasted into an AI tool
Explain how hallucination, bias and deepfakes can cause harm
Describe when and how to disclose AI use at work or school
Write a short personal AI-use policy you can follow

lessons.title: What not to paste in

blocks.text: When you type or paste something into an online AI tool, you are sending it to a company's servers. What happens next depends on the tool, your account type and your settings. Some services may store conversations, let staff review them, or use them to improve their systems unless you switch that off. Others, usually business plans, make firmer promises. You cannot see any of this from the chat window.
So the safest rule is simple. Do not paste anything you would not be comfortable seeing leave your control.

blocks.caption: Sort your information
rows: Personal information
ID numbers, home addresses, phone numbers, medical details, photos of other people
Remove, or replace with placeholders
Client and customer data
Names with order details, invoices, complaints, student records
Anonymise, or do not paste
Financial details
Bank account and card numbers, passwords, tax records, payslips
Never paste
Confidential business material
Unreleased plans, contracts, staff reviews, supplier prices
Check your workplace rules first
Public or invented information
A published article, a made-up example, your own general question
Generally fine

blocks.title: Swap the details, keep the task
blocks.text: A bookkeeper wants help wording a payment reminder. Instead of pasting the client's invoice, she writes: 'Client A, invoice for R12 400, 30 days overdue, regular customer, polite but firm.' She gets a good draft, then adds the real name and amount herself. The assistant never saw either.
Anonymise before you paste

items.title: Strip the identifiers
items.text: Remove names, ID and account numbers, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and anything that points to one person.

items.title: Use placeholders
items.text: Write Client A, Staff member B, [amount] and [date]. Put the real details back after.

items.title: Keep only what the task needs
items.text: Paste the paragraph that matters, not the whole document or email chain.

blocks.text: Laws and workplace rules

Many countries regulate how personal information may be handled. In South Africa, that includes the Protection of Personal Information Act, usually called POPIA. You do not need to know the detail to use a good rule: if the information is about identifiable people who did not agree to it being shared with a tool like this, think twice.
Your employer or school may also have its own policy, including approved tools. Find it and follow it. If there is no policy, ask.

blocks.title: Free is not private
blocks.text: Never assume a free tool treats your data the way a paid business tool might. Read the privacy settings and what the provider says about storing and reusing conversations. If you cannot find a clear answer, treat the chat as semi-public.

blocks.title: Clean up a risky prompt
blocks.intro: Paper or screen. No AI tool is needed.
tasks: Take this prompt: 'Write a letter to Mrs Dlamini, ID 7203150123083, at 14 Protea Road, telling her that her account 4012 3456 is R3 200 overdue.' Rewrite it so no private detail remains.
List what you would now add back by hand, after you have the draft.
Look at your last three prompts to any AI tool. Mark anything you would remove if you did them again.
Find the privacy or data-use settings in one tool you use, and note what they say about your conversations.
blocks.reflection: Which kind of information did you find easiest to forget about when you were in a hurry?
