blocks.prompt: What is the safest way to get help wording a reminder to an overdue client?
options: Describe the situation with placeholders and add real names and amounts yourself
Paste the client's full invoice with their account details
Share a photo of the signed contract
Include the client's ID number so the draft is accurate
blocks.explain: Placeholders give the assistant what it needs for wording while keeping personal and financial details out of the tool.

lessons.title: Hallucination, bias and deepfakes

blocks.text: Earlier in the course you met hallucination, where a model produces fluent text that is false. Here is how that and two other limitations turn into real-world harm.
Hallucination in the real world

The harm comes from trust. A wrong figure goes into a quote. An invented rule goes into a staff notice. A made-up reference goes into an assignment. In each case, someone relied on text that looked authoritative. In some fields, such as law, medicine and finance, relying on a wrong answer can have serious consequences, which is why a qualified person must check anything that matters.
Bias

Models learn from human writing, and human writing contains stereotypes, gaps and unequal attention. The result is that AI output can reflect those patterns. It may assume a nurse is a woman and an engineer is a man, describe some groups more negatively than others, or know far more about some countries and languages than about others. It may handle English better than isiZulu or Sesotho, and writing about African contexts may be thinner or more generic.

blocks.title: A job advert gone wrong
blocks.text: A small agency asks an assistant to write a job advert and a shortlist guide. The draft describes the ideal candidate as 'young, energetic and a native English speaker'. That is not a requirement for the role, and it may be unfair or unlawful. A person reading it critically caught it. Anyone just pressing send would not have.

You cannot remove bias from a tool. You can notice it, ask for neutral wording, and keep humans responsible for decisions about people. Do not let AI output alone decide who gets hired, graded, promoted or refused.
Deepfakes and fake content

A deepfake is an image, video or audio clip made or altered by AI to show someone saying or doing something they never did. Voices can be cloned from short recordings. Fake photos can look real at a glance. These are used for scams, harassment and false news.

items: A voice note that sounds like your boss asking for an urgent payment.
A video of a public figure endorsing a get-rich-quick scheme.
A convincing screenshot of a conversation that never happened.

blocks.title: Slow down and verify another way
blocks.text: If a message asks for money, passwords or secrecy, contact the person on a number you already have. Look for the original source of a clip. Be wary of content that is designed to make you angry or afraid, and do not forward it until you have checked.

blocks.title: Do not make them
blocks.text: Never create a deepfake of a real person without their clear permission. Doing so can harm them and may be against the law or against the rules of a school, employer or platform.

blocks.prompt: You receive a voice note that sounds like your manager, asking you to pay a supplier urgently into a new account. What is the best response?
options: Confirm by calling your manager on a number you already know before doing anything
Pay immediately, since voice notes cannot be faked
Reply to the same voice note asking if it is really them
Forward it to colleagues to see what they think
blocks.explain: Voices can be cloned. Verifying through a separate, trusted channel protects you, while replying in the same thread leaves you talking to the sender.

lessons.title: Disclosure and your personal AI-use policy

blocks.text: Using AI is rarely the problem. Hiding it where people expect you to be open about it is. Disclosure is simply telling the people who rely on your work how it was made, so they can judge it properly.
When to say you used it

items: At school or university: follow your institution's rules. Some allow AI for brainstorming but not for writing, some require a note, and some ban it for certain tasks. Presenting AI-written work as your own where it is not allowed is cheating, however good the text.
At work: check the policy, and tell your manager or client if AI shaped a deliverable they are paying for, especially if their contract or rules say something about it.
In public content: a short note is good practice when AI generated an image, voice or large parts of a text.
Whenever someone asks you directly: tell the truth.

blocks.title: Two ways to hand in the same report
blocks.text: Thabo drafts a report, uses an assistant to tidy his grammar, and checks every fact. His manager has said light editing help is fine, so he sends it as is. Lerato asks the assistant to write the whole report from scratch, does not read it closely, and sends it with an invented statistic inside. Both used AI. Only one was responsible for the result.

blocks.title: You are accountable
blocks.text: Whatever tool helped, the name on the work is yours. If it is wrong, you answer for it, not the software.
A personal AI-use policy
A policy sounds formal, but yours can fit on a card. Writing it down in advance means you decide calmly, not under deadline pressure.

blocks.label: Template: my AI-use policy
blocks.text:
1. I will not paste: [personal, client, financial or confidential information].
2. I will always check: [figures, names, dates, quotes, anything that could cost money or hurt someone].
3. I will not use AI for: [tasks that must be my own work, or that need a qualified expert].
4. I will disclose AI use when: [school or work rules ask, or the reader would reasonably expect to know].
5. If I am unsure, I will: [ask my manager, teacher or client before using it].

blocks.title: Write your policy
blocks.intro: Fill in the template for your own situation. Keep it to one page.
tasks: Complete all five lines using real examples from your own work or study.
Find your school's or employer's rule on AI, or write down who you could ask.
Add one line about image or voice content if you create it.
Put the finished policy somewhere you will see it, such as the first page of your notes app or a card on your desk.
Offline option: write it by hand and stick it above your workspace.
blocks.reflection: Which line in your policy will be hardest to keep when you are tired and under deadline, and what small habit would support it?

blocks.prompt: Which description best fits a responsible approach to using AI in assessed work?
options: Follow the stated rules, check every claim and be open about any AI help the rules require you to mention
Use it freely and hope nobody asks about it
Avoid reading the rules so you can say you did not know
Present the AI output as your own because you typed the request
blocks.explain: Responsible use means following the rules, checking what you submit, and disclosing as required. Responsibility for the final work stays with you.

modules.title: Building practical AI workflows
modules.summary: Turn a repeated job into a reliable process: split it into steps, decide who does what, reuse templates, review the output and measure the time you save.
objectives: Break a job into clear steps and decide which are done by AI and which by a person
Build a reusable prompt template with placeholders
Apply a review checklist before using AI output
Measure time saved honestly and design a workflow for your own work

lessons.title: Break the job into steps and split the work

blocks.text: Up to now you have used AI one task at a time. The real gains come when you take a job you repeat, such as a weekly client update or monthly quotes, and turn it into a small, dependable process. A workflow is just that: a sequence of steps, with a clear owner for each.
The key move is to stop asking 'Can AI do this job?' and start asking 'Which parts of this job can AI help with, and which parts must stay with me?' Almost every job contains both.

items.title: Pick one repeated job
items.text: Choose something you do at least weekly, that is mostly language or organising, and that does not carry high risk.

items.title: Write down the steps as you do them today
items.text: Be honest and specific. Include the boring bits, like finding the file or checking the price list.

items.title: Mark each step: AI, human or both
items.text: Use the questions below to decide.

items.title: Define the input and the output of each step
items.text: What goes in, and what should come out, in what format?

items.title: Add a review point
items.text: Decide where a person checks before anything reaches a customer or a decision.

items.title: Test it on real work and adjust
items.text: Run it two or three times and fix what breaks.

blocks.text: Who does which step

blocks.caption: A simple way to divide the work
rows: First drafts and rewording
Decisions, prices and promises
Sorting, summarising and reformatting text you supplied
Facts that must be right: figures, dates, names
Generating options to choose from
Anything involving private or sensitive information
Spotting gaps by asking questions
Sensitive conversations and relationships
Turning notes into a template
Final approval and sending

blocks.title: A tutor's weekly parent update
blocks.text: Naledi tutors six learners. Her old routine: remember how each session went, write a message to each parent, find the homework page, send on WhatsApp. It took about 90 minutes on Sunday. Her workflow: she types three rough bullets per learner (the human step, because only she knows how the session went). The assistant turns each set into a warm, short message in a fixed format (the AI step). She reads each one, corrects anything wrong and adds a personal line (the review step), then sends them herself (the human step). Her step list is now one page, and she knows exactly where a mistake could creep in.

blocks.title: Start small
blocks.text: Automate nothing you do not understand. Run the workflow by hand with a chat assistant for a few weeks before thinking about tools that connect apps and send things for you. Anything that sends messages without a person looking at them needs far more care.

blocks.prompt: In a good AI workflow, which step should normally stay with a person?
options: Final approval and sending of anything that reaches a customer
Rewording a rough note into a cleaner sentence
Sorting a pasted list into categories
Producing three alternative subject lines
blocks.explain: Drafting and sorting suit AI help. A person should approve and send, because accountability for what reaches other people stays with them.

lessons.title: Templates, a review checklist and time saved

blocks.text: A workflow that you re-invent every week is not much of a workflow. Three habits make it repeatable: a reusable prompt template, a review checklist and a simple measure of time saved.
Reusable prompt templates
Take a prompt that worked and swap the details that change for placeholders in square brackets. You are left with a fill-in-the-blanks form. Next week you only supply the new facts.

blocks.label: Template: weekly parent update
blocks.text:
I am a maths tutor. Write a WhatsApp message to the parent of [learner name], Grade [grade]. Use only the notes below.
Notes: [3 bullet points about this week]
Homework: [what and by when]
Tone: warm, honest and brief. Under 70 words. No promises about marks. If anything is missing, write [missing] instead of guessing.

Keep templates in one place, such as a notes app or a document, with a title and a line about when to use each. Update the template whenever you find a fix, and the next run starts from the better version.
A review checklist
The review step is where most of the value and most of the risk sits. A short checklist stops you skimming. Print it, or keep it beside the template.

blocks.label: Review checklist
blocks.text:
[ ] Facts: names, dates, amounts and promises match my notes
[ ] Nothing invented: no extra offers, claims, sources or statistics
[ ] Private details: nothing sensitive went in, nothing sensitive came out
[ ] Tone: sounds like me and suits the reader
[ ] Fairness: no assumptions about age, gender, language or background
[ ] Purpose: it does what I need and nothing more
[ ] Rules: allowed under my school or workplace policy
Measuring time saved
Do not guess. Time the old way for one or two rounds, then time the new way, including the review. Count everything: preparing notes, running the prompt, checking, fixing and sending.

blocks.caption: A simple time record
rows: Minutes per run
Runs per month
Minutes per month
Saved per month
220 minutes, about 3.7 hours

blocks.title: Count the hidden costs
blocks.text: If the AI draft needs so much correction that you spend as long fixing it as writing it, the workflow is not saving time. That is a useful result too. Change the template, change the step, or stop using AI for that job.

blocks.title: Quality counts too
blocks.text: Time saved is only one measure. Note any change in mistakes, customer replies or stress. A workflow that is fast and gets more errors is worse than the old one.

blocks.prompt: Why should you time the review and fixing steps when measuring a new AI workflow?
options: They are part of the real cost, so leaving them out overstates the time saved
They are optional and rarely affect the total
Only the AI drafting time matters in the comparison
They always take zero minutes once you have a template
blocks.explain: The workflow includes checking and correcting. If you leave those out, the figures flatter the process and hide whether it is actually helping.

lessons.title: Capstone: design a workflow for your own work

blocks.text: This lesson pulls the whole course into one piece of practical work. You will design a complete workflow for something you really do, in your job, studies, household admin or small business. No new theory is needed. You already have the parts: knowing what AI is good and bad at, writing a clear prompt, checking facts, protecting private information and being honest about how you used it.
Choose well

Good first candidates are repeated, language-heavy and low-risk: weekly updates, quote drafts, social post batches, meeting follow-ups, study summaries, customer replies. Poor first candidates involve sensitive personal data, legal or medical advice, or decisions about people.

blocks.title: Three possible choices
blocks.text: A freelance photographer: turn a booking enquiry into a quote and a confirmation message. A student: turn lecture notes into a revision summary and ten practice questions each week. A shop owner: turn the week's stock notes into a supplier order email and a customer announcement.

blocks.title: Capstone: design your AI workflow
blocks.intro: Work on paper or in a document. If you have a free AI chat tool, use it for steps 5 and 6. You can complete the whole design without one.
tasks: Name the job and who it is for. Describe it in two sentences, including how often you do it and how long it takes now. Record the time honestly.
List the steps as you do them today, in order. Aim for five to eight steps.
Mark each step as AI, human or both. Write one sentence of reasoning for any step you give to AI. Remove or protect any private data before it reaches a tool.

Write the input and the expected output for each AI step. Then write one reusable prompt template with at least three placeholders. Use the ingredients from Module 4: context, task, audience, format, constraints.
Add a review point. Copy the review checklist and adapt it with at least two items specific to your job, such as a figure that must match your price list.
Test it with one real example (with private details removed). Time the new way from start to finish, including review. Note what the assistant got wrong and fix your template.
Write a short disclosure line, if one is needed, and one line of your personal AI-use policy that applies to this job.
Summarise in three lines: time before, time after, and the one mistake your checklist caught.
blocks.reflection: If your workflow saved you no time, which step would you redesign first? And what would you tell a friend who wanted to copy your workflow, including the warnings?

blocks.title: Keep the version history
blocks.text: Save your template and checklist with a date. After a month, look back at what you changed. The improvements show you what you learned about your own work, and the tool, in that time.

You have now covered the whole path: what AI is, how it works, how to ask it well, where it helps, where it harms and how to put it into a routine you control. The next step is the one that matters most. Use it on real work, check it carefully and keep adjusting.

blocks.prompt: Which job makes the best first candidate for an AI workflow?
options: A weekly, language-heavy task with low risk, such as drafting routine customer updates
A one-off legal dispute that needs precise wording
Deciding which staff member to dismiss
Storing clients' bank details in a chat to save time
blocks.explain: Repeated, language-based and low-risk jobs offer clear gains and limit the cost of mistakes. Legal, personnel and financial-data tasks need qualified people or strict protection.

furtherLearning: Practise one workflow from Module 10 on real work for a month, then refine your templates.
Read your school's, employer's or industry body's current guidance on AI use and keep your personal policy up to date.
Explore a free course on data basics or spreadsheets to check AI-generated numbers more confidently.
Try a digital safety course to sharpen your instincts about scams, deepfakes and account security.
